title: WebSocket Design Patterns
explain: To push messages to millions of connected users, I put a fleet of stateless WebSocket gateway nodes behind an L4 load balancer, keep a registry of which node holds which user's connection, and deliver through an outbox, Kafka and a router that looks the user up and sends to that exact node. Offline users go to an inbox and catch up by sequence number on reconnect.
model:
```
User -> L4 LB (TCP passthrough) -> GW node (conn pinned there, ~50k each)
                                       |  conn_id -> socket (in memory)
                                       v
                    Registry (Redis): user_id -> {gw_node, conn_id, epoch}, TTL by heartbeat

Service --(state + outbox row, one txn)--> DB --> Relay (poll/CDC) --> Kafka (key = user_id)
   --> Delivery Router --lookup--> GW node --> socket     (offline/stale -> Inbox + mobile push)
```

**Two mappings:** the global `user -> gw_node` in Redis (the Router picks a node) and the local `conn_id -> socket` in node memory (the node finds the socket).

**Send path.**

1. Service writes state **and** an outbox row in one transaction.
2. Relay publishes to Kafka with `key = user_id` (per-user order), marks sent.
3. Router consumes, looks up `carol -> gw-3 / c31 / epoch 5`.
4. Router sends to gw-3 (gRPC or pub/sub `ch:gw-3`) with `conn_id` and `epoch`.
5. gw-3 pushes `{seq, payload}` on that socket.

**Offline or stale:** no entry, or the node answers `NOT_OWNER`: store in the **inbox** plus mobile push. The user reconnects to any node, the epoch increments, the client sends `last_seq`, and the inbox replays the rest.

GW nodes hold no durable state, so they scale out and can be killed; their TTLs expire and users reconnect elsewhere.

details.q: Why an L4 load balancer, and what does that imply for routing?
details.a: WebSocket connections are long-lived TCP, so the LB just passes bytes through (least-connections) and each connection stays pinned to one GW node for its lifetime. You therefore cannot reach a user through any node: you must know which node holds the connection, which is what the registry is for.

The registry is global (`user_id -> gw_node, conn_id, epoch`, with a TTL renewed by heartbeat) so the Router can choose a node. The `conn_id -> socket` table is local to the node because a socket object cannot be shared. Keeping sockets out of the registry also keeps the registry small and cheap to update.

They act as a [fencing token](#/sd/f/fencing-token) for connection ownership. Carol moves from gw-3 (epoch 5) to gw-1 (epoch 6); a Router with a stale lookup sends to gw-3 with epoch 5, and gw-3 answers `NOT_OWNER` instead of pushing to a dead or superseded connection. The Router re-resolves or falls back to the inbox.

details.q: Why write an outbox row instead of publishing to Kafka directly from the service?
details.a: Publishing after the commit can lose the message on a crash; publishing before can announce state that never committed. The outbox puts the state change and its message in one transaction, and a relay (poll or CDC, see [change feed](#/sd/f/change-feed)) publishes it later. The pipeline is then at-least-once.

details.q: The pipeline is at-least-once. What does the client do?
details.a: Every message carries a per-user `seq`. The client dedupes by seq and detects gaps: after processing 41 it receives 43, so it requests a resend from 41 (or replays from the inbox) before acking, and drops a late duplicate 42 once applied. Acking 43 blindly would hide the loss.

details.q: Dave is offline. What happens to a message for him, and what happens when he comes back?
details.a: His registry entry has expired, so the Router writes the message to his inbox (and sends APNs/FCM if appropriate). When he reconnects, possibly to a different node, that node writes a new registry entry with epoch + 1, the client sends `last_seq`, and the inbox replays what it missed.

details.q: How many gateway nodes for 10 million concurrent users if a node handles at most 50,000 connections and you run at 70%?
details.a: At 70% a node carries 35,000, so 10,000,000 / 35,000 = 285.7, round up to 286 nodes. The headroom absorbs reconnect storms and the loss of a node.

details.q: Alternative: each node subscribes to a per-user pub/sub channel for its connected users. Trade-off?
details.a: It removes the registry lookup at send time, but routing state does not disappear: it moves into the subscription table, with one subscription per online user (here 10 M) that must move on every reconnect. Lookup costs a read per message; subscriptions cost memory and churn proportional to online users.

prompts.q: Walk through the path of a message to an online user, end to end.
points: State and outbox row in one transaction
Relay to Kafka keyed by user_id for per-user order
Router looks up user in the registry
Targeted delivery to that GW node with conn_id and epoch
GW finds the socket in memory and pushes {seq, payload}

prompts.q: What happens when the user is offline, or has just moved to another node?
points: Expired or missing registry entry goes to inbox plus mobile push
Stale route gets NOT_OWNER thanks to epoch fencing
Reconnect to any node bumps epoch and rewrites the registry
Client sends last_seq and the inbox replays the gap

prompts.q: What delivery guarantee does the system give and how does the client cope?
points: At-least-once end to end via outbox
Client dedupes and detects gaps before acking
Order preserved per user by Kafka key

prompts.q: Compare registry lookup per message with per-user pub/sub channels, and size the gateway fleet for 10 M users.
points: Registry: one read per message, small routing state
Pub/sub: no lookup, but one subscription per online user to maintain
Nodes are stateless and scale out; killed nodes expire by TTL
10 M / (50k x 70%) is about 286 nodes, with headroom for reconnect storms
